newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korea unveils plans to boost competitiveness.
newsitem.headline: South Korea unveils plans to boost competitiveness.

text.p: South Korea announced measures on Wednesday to boost its sagging economy, including slashing domestic steel prices and opening power production to private sector competition.
The Finance and Economy Ministry said private companies would be allowed to compete with the state Korea Electric Power Corp (KEPCO) on non-nuclear power production, but it did not give a timetable.
But KEPCO would retain its monopoly on power distribution, a ministry statement said.

It said Pohang Iron and Steel Co (POSCO), 20 percent-owned by the government, would cut the domestic sales price of hot coiled steel from the end of this month by eight percent from its current 256,000 won per tonne.

Restrictions on large firms seeking overseas borrowings will be lifted if their purchases of locally-produced equipment in the previous year meet government requirements. The timetable, however, would be announced later.
Currently, only small and medium-sized firms can access foreign loans to finance capital goods purchases.
But the package did not mention any easing in reserve requirement ratios for banks despite widespread market speculation that the package would include a cut in the ratio.
The statement said the government would gradually increase key energy prices to encourage energy conservation.
The government also plans to reduce the government sector workforce by about 10,000 over the next four years.
The statement also reaffirmed the government's commitment to deregulating the domestic financial industry, which analysts say is still under strict official controls.
The government will ease rules on new entries into the land freight transport business. South Korean companies currently face the highest distribution costs among Asian nations, it said.
Local governments will be selectively allowed to receive foreign loans to finance infrastructure projects, a plan also aimed at reducing distribution costs, it said.
